Facing Eviction in Spain: A Guide for Tenants and Landlords


Eviction can be a stressful experience for both tenants and landlords in Spain.
This guide offers an overview of the eviction process in Spain, but remember, it’s not a substitute for legal advice.


For Tenants:


Understanding When Eviction is Possible: Landlords can only evict you under specific legal justifications outlined in the Urban Lease Law (Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos – LAU). These include:

  • Non-payment of rent (typically exceeding one month’s rent in arrears)
  • Breach of contract (causing significant damage, illegal activities, unauthorized subletting)
  • End of a fixed-term contract (landlord doesn’t wish to renew)
  • Landlord’s needs (with strict notice periods and potential compensation)


Protecting Your Rights:

  • Right to Legal Defence: You have the right to legal representation throughout the process.
  • Dispute Over Rent Amount: If you believe the rent is unfair or exceeds legal limitations, you might have grounds to contest it in court.
  • Vulnerable Circumstances: Social services might intervene and offer temporary alternative housing solutions in cases of economic hardship or vulnerability.


Seeking Help and Resources:

  • Legal Aid: Spain offers legal aid programs for low-income individuals.
  • Tenant Associations: Local tenant associations can provide support and guidance.
  • Social Services: Depending on your situation, social services might offer temporary housing assistance.

Early Communication is Key: If you’re facing financial difficulties that might lead to late rent payments, try to reach an agreement with your landlord as soon as possible.


For Landlords:


Grounds for Eviction: You can initiate eviction proceedings only under specific legal reasons outlined in the LAU (mentioned above).

The Eviction Process:

  • Issue a formal demand for payment of outstanding rent or a notice to vacate.
  • If the tenant fails to comply, initiate legal proceedings through the court system.
  • Obtain a court order for eviction if the judge rules in your favour.
  • Enforce the eviction order with the involvement of law enforcement (final stage).


Considerations:

Eviction can be a lengthy and costly process. Consider alternative solutions like mediation before resorting to eviction.

You are obligated to comply with the terms of the tenancy agreement, including repairs and maintenance responsibilities.


Remember:

  • Communication is crucial for both parties. Open communication can help resolve issues and potentially avoid the eviction process.
  • This guide offers a general overview, and the specifics can vary depending on the circumstances. Consulting with a lawyer specializing in rental law is highly recommended for both tenants and landlords to understand your rights and options in a specific situation.

The specific circumstances surrounding eviction proceedings in Spain can vary depending on the nature of the tenancy agreement (Arrendamiento de Vivienda, Contrato de Temporada, etc.), the reason for eviction, and the applicable version of the Urban Lease Law (LAU).


We strongly recommend consulting with a qualified legal professional specializing in Spanish property law to ensure you fully understand your rights and obligations as a tenant or landlord in a specific eviction scenario. A lawyer can provide tailored advice based on the details of your situation and help you navigate the legalities involved.
